what: Commercial Metals makes steel from scrap. It recycles metal in its own yards, melts it in electric arc furnaces and rolls it into rebar, merchant bar and steel mesh, most of which goes into concrete construction. It also fabricates and installs the finished steel on site and sells engineered building solutions.
customers: Construction contractors, infrastructure projects, fabricators and distributors in North America, plus a sizeable operation in Poland serving central Europe.
money: Rebar and merchant bar from scrap-fed mills, plus downstream fabrication and installation.
Polish mills serving central European construction.
Engineered solutions including ground stabilisation and construction products.
moat: Rebar is heavy, cheap per tonne and expensive to transport, so the market is regional and whoever has the nearest mill wins. Commercial Metals owns the scrap supply ahead of the mill and the fabrication business behind it, which means it captures margin at three stages of the same tonne. Electric arc furnaces also cost far less to idle than blast furnaces, so downturns hurt it much less than they hurt integrated steelmakers.
risks: Steel pricing drives earnings, and the metal spread between scrap cost and finished steel price can compress quickly.
Construction activity is interest-rate sensitive, and non-residential building has been soft.
Debt of $3.6B against $778.9M of cash has risen with acquisitions in the engineered solutions businesses.
Revenue was flat to falling for three years, from $8.9B to $7.8B, before the recent recovery to $9.4B.
Imported rebar competes on price whenever trade enforcement weakens, and the trade position can change with administrations.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 10.0 times earnings, 0.67 times sales and 8.2 times EV/EBITDA, undemanding for a business this well positioned.
Infrastructure spending programmes feed demand for exactly the products Commercial Metals makes, and bridges and roads consume rebar by the tonne.
Free cash flow of $479.1M against a $6.3B market value funds buybacks that have steadily reduced the share count.
Electric arc furnace steelmaking has a structural cost and carbon advantage over blast furnaces, and that gap widens as emissions rules tighten.
Eleven analysts average a $78.00 target, about 36% above the current price.
watch: The metal margin: finished steel price minus scrap cost per tonne. Everything else in this business is a function of that spread and the tonnes shipped through it.
view: Commercial Metals is the quiet one in American steel, and the better business for it. While the integrated producers fight over automotive sheet with blast furnaces that cost a fortune to idle, CMC melts scrap into rebar in regional mini-mills, sells it into construction within a few hundred miles, and then fabricates and installs it too. That last part matters more than it sounds: owning the scrap yard in front of the mill and the fabrication shop behind it means the company earns on the same tonne three times, which is why its margins through the cycle have been more stable than any peer except Nucor.

The electric arc furnace point deserves emphasis because it is the structural reason to prefer this to Cleveland-Cliffs. An EAF can be turned down when demand falls and restarted cheaply; a blast furnace cannot, which is why integrated steelmakers post enormous losses in downturns and scrap-based producers post small profits. Add that scrap-fed steel carries a fraction of the carbon intensity of the blast furnace route, and the regulatory direction of travel is a tailwind rather than a liability. None of this is new information, but it is consistently underweighted when people price steel companies off the same cycle.

At 10 times earnings, 0.67 times sales and 8.2 times EV/EBITDA, you are not being asked to pay for any of it. The market treats CMC as a cyclical commodity producer at a moment when non-residential construction is weak and rates are high, and prices it accordingly. What it is actually underwriting is a regionally protected, vertically integrated business selling into infrastructure programmes that have years of funded work behind them, generating $479 million of free cash flow against a $6.3 billion market value and using it to shrink the share count. That is a reasonable thing to own at this multiple even if steel prices go nowhere.

The risk is the one that always applies: the metal margin. Earnings here are the spread between scrap cost and finished steel price multiplied by tonnes, and that spread can halve in two quarters if imports arrive or construction stalls. The $3.6 billion of debt taken on for the engineered-solutions acquisitions is the part of the story I would scrutinise hardest, because buying higher-multiple adjacent businesses with borrowed money is how good steel companies have historically turned themselves into mediocre conglomerates. So far the record is fine. Watch the metal margin, watch whether the acquired businesses earn their cost of capital, and treat the eleven analysts’ $78 target as directionally sensible rather than precise.
bull: Infrastructure demand holds the metal margin while fabrication and engineered solutions lift the blended return, and buybacks compound a cheap multiple.
bear: Non-residential construction stalls, imported rebar pressures price, and the spread compresses while $3.6 billion of acquisition debt still has to be serviced.
